channel.title: AstroAlert – what's happening in space
channel.description: A daily updated guide to astronomical and space events: eclipses, conjunctions, meteor showers, rocket launches, aurorae and close approaches of asteroids.

item.title: Draconids meteor shower peak
item.description:
08.10.2027, 02:00 UTC

An unpredictable shower: usually weak, but a few times in history it has produced genuine meteor storms. The radiant is already high in the early evening. At maximum, up to 10 meteors per hour in theory (the ZHR – under a perfectly dark sky with the radiant overhead; in practice usually several times fewer). The radiant lies in Draco. A Moon 56% illuminated will brighten the sky a little. No equipment needed – just a reclining chair, warm clothes and a spot away from city lights.

item.title: Asteroid 465824 (2010 FR) passes by
item.description:
11.09.2026, 22:28 UTC

An asteroid with an estimated diameter of 122–273 m will pass Earth at 7.76 million km, or 20.2 times the Earth–Moon distance, travelling at 11.6 km/s. For scale: roughly the size of a small hill. This is not a close encounter – it makes the list as one of the largest objects passing us this week. NASA classifies it as “potentially hazardous” – but that is purely a technical category for objects larger than about 140 m whose orbits come close to Earth's. No known object threatens us in the foreseeable future.

Object record in the JPL database

item.title: Asteroid 2014 FV32 passes by
item.description:
10.09.2026, 17:28 UTC

An asteroid with an estimated diameter of 80–179 m will pass Earth at 12.28 million km, or 32.0 times the Earth–Moon distance, travelling at 10.6 km/s. For scale: roughly the size of a large apartment block. This is not a close encounter – it makes the list as one of the largest objects passing us this week. The pass is entirely safe – approaches like this happen regularly and are tracked as a matter of routine.

item.description:
31.10.2026, 00:00 UTC

Mission: 35th commercial resupply services mission to the International Space Station operated by SpaceX. The flight will be conducted under the second Commercial Resupply Services contract with NASA. Cargo Dragon 2 brings supplies and payloads, including critical materials to directly support science and research investigations that occur onboard the orbiting laboratory. item.title: Neptune at opposition
item.description:
28.09.2027, 14:01 UTC

Neptune lies opposite the Sun – it rises at sunset, culminates around midnight and shines at its brightest of the season. Distance from Earth: 28.86 au (4,317 million km; its light takes 240 minutes to reach us). The planet is in Pisces. A telescope target only.

item.title: Perseids meteor shower peak
item.description:
12.08.2027, 02:00 UTC

The most popular shower of the year – it falls in the holiday season and on warm nights. Its source is comet 109P/Swift-Tuttle. At maximum, up to 100 meteors per hour in theory (the ZHR – under a perfectly dark sky with the radiant overhead; in practice usually several times fewer). The radiant lies in Perseus. Unfortunately the Moon will be 77% illuminated and will drown out the fainter meteors – it is worth observing after it sets. No equipment needed – just a reclining chair, warm clothes and a spot away from city lights.

item.title: Total solar eclipse – the longest of the century
item.description:
02.08.2027, 10:07 UTC

Totality lasts 6 minutes and 23 seconds – the longest eclipse visible from land in the 21st century and indeed until 2114. The path runs across southern Spain and North Africa, passing over Luxor among other places. WARNING: never look at the Sun without certified solar filters – sunglasses or exposed film do NOT protect your eyes.

Details and visibility map (NASA)

item.title: Delta Aquariids meteor shower peak
item.description:
30.07.2027, 02:00 UTC

A gentle maximum spread over several nights, best seen from southern latitudes. At maximum, up to 25 meteors per hour in theory (the ZHR – under a perfectly dark sky with the radiant overhead; in practice usually several times fewer). The radiant lies in Aquarius. Conditions are excellent – the Moon will barely interfere. No equipment needed – just a reclining chair, warm clothes and a spot away from city lights.
